title: Make Activities for Everyone
subtitle: Learn to adapt plans so everyone can join in and have fun.
objectives: Identify parts of an activity that might unintentionally exclude someone.
Suggest alternative ways for people to contribute to an activity.
Explain how to ask participants for their preferences to ensure inclusion.

scenes.title: Ready to Play?
scenes.narration: Planning a game means everyone should have fun. Sometimes, plans unintentionally exclude. Let's learn to make every activity a blast for all participants.
scenes.visualAction: Animated characters excitedly gather, then one character looks a bit left out.

scenes.title: What is Inclusion?
scenes.narration: Inclusion means everyone feels welcome and participates fully. Offer different ways to do things. This ensures no one is left out, enriching the experience for all.
scenes.visualAction: The left-out character is now included in the group, smiling. A thought bubble appears with diverse activity options.

scenes.title: A Team Game Challenge
scenes.narration: For a team game, running might exclude some. Offer alternatives like seated clue solving or reading aloud. Everyone still helps the team!
scenes.visualAction: A cartoon character runs, then the scene changes to show characters doing different activities: one reading, one writing, one pointing, all contributing to a central 'clue board'.

scenes.title: Key Steps to Inclusion
scenes.narration: To make activities inclusive: Check for exclusions, ask participants what works, then offer meaningful alternatives. It's about teamwork and respect.
scenes.visualAction: Three distinct icons appear: a magnifying glass (check), a speech bubble (ask), and multiple paths (offer).

scenes.title: Improving a Prompt
scenes.narration: AI ideas might not be inclusive initially. Improve your prompt! Ask for options for different abilities and preferences. A good prompt helps.
scenes.visualAction: A text box shows a simple prompt, then transforms into a more detailed, inclusive prompt with different options highlighted.

scenes.title: Your Turn to Plan
scenes.narration: Now, adapt an activity idea. Offer different ways for people to participate. Use the 'Check, Ask, Offer' steps we just learned. You can do it!
scenes.visualAction: A character holds a clipboard and pencil, looking thoughtful. Another character gives a thumbs-up.

scenes.title: Celebrate Inclusion!
scenes.narration: Fantastic! You've learned to make activities welcoming. Inclusion makes games more creative and fun for everyone. Keep practicing these skills!
scenes.visualAction: All characters from previous scenes are together, celebrating with confetti falling. The previously left-out character is central and happy.

reading.title: What is an Inclusive Activity?
reading.text: An inclusive activity is designed so that everyone can participate and feel welcome, regardless of their abilities or preferences. It means thinking about different ways people can join in and contribute. The goal is to avoid unintentionally excluding anyone and to make the experience enjoyable for all involved.

reading.title: Adapting a Game
reading.text: The suggestion assumes one ability and preference for everyone. Ask what suits participants and review the ways to contribute. These roles contribute to the team's goal, and participants are asked what suits them rather than assigned assumed preferences.

reading.title: How to Check for Inclusion
reading.text: To check if an activity is inclusive, first review its steps for any hidden assumptions about what people can or want to do. Then, ask the actual participants for their ideas and preferences. Never guess or assume someone's ability or preference based on their appearance or background. Offer choices!

materials.title: Invented Teaching Example: Original Team Game Proposal
materials.text: Game: The Great Clue Hunt!Objective: Teams race to find hidden clues around the park and solve a puzzle.Rules: All team members must run to each clue location, read the clue, and bring it back to the starting point. The first team to solve the puzzle wins.Equipment: Clues, park map, running shoes.This proposal assumes everyone can run quickly and enjoys doing so. It might exclude friends who prefer other ways to contribute.

promptExamples.initial: Plan a fun outdoor game for a group of friends.
promptExamples.improved: Plan a fun outdoor game for a group of friends, making sure there are different ways for everyone to participate, including options for those who prefer less physical activity or have different strengths. Ask for specific roles.
promptExamples.followup: How can we make sure the 'clue reader' role is just as exciting and important as the 'clue runner' role?

activity.title: Make it Inclusive!
activity.instructions: Read the activity description below. Then, rewrite it to make it more inclusive, offering at least two different ways for people to participate. Explain who might benefit from each alternative.
activity.starter: Activity: The Great Clue Hunt! Instructions: Teams race to find hidden clues around the park and solve a puzzle. All team members must run to each clue location, read the clue, and bring it back to the starting point. The first team to solve the puzzle wins.
activity.expectedEvidence: A rewritten activity description that includes alternative participation methods and explains their benefits.

quiz.question: A game suggestion says, 'Everyone must run to collect clues.' Which assumption needs checking?
options: That everyone can and wants to run.
That the game has a name.
quiz.explanation: The suggestion assumes one ability and preference for everyone. Ask what suits participants and review the ways to contribute.

quiz.question: How could you adapt the game while keeping meaningful participation?
options: Offer clue solving, reading, recording and optional movement, then ask participants to choose.
Let anyone who does not want to run only watch.
quiz.explanation: These roles contribute to the team's goal, and participants are asked what suits them rather than assigned assumed preferences.

quiz.question: In an imaginary art club, someone says, 'I prefer describing an idea aloud.' What should you do?
options: Exclude them from developing the idea.
Agree on a useful description role and ask whether it suits them.
quiz.explanation: Respect the stated preference and agree on a meaningful contribution. Do not infer ability or decide for someone without asking.

mission.title: Design an Inclusive Art Club
mission.instructions: Design an imaginary group art activity with at least 3 useful roles. Explain each role's contribution and write a question inviting people to choose what suits them or suggest an adjustment. Do not assign roles based on appearance or names.
rubric: At least 3 roles make a meaningful contribution.
Participants are asked what suits them and can request adjustments.
Roles are offered without assumptions about ability or preference.

hints.question: How do I know if my activity is inclusive?
hints.answer: Check if your activity makes any assumptions about what people can or want to do. If it only offers one way to participate, it might not be inclusive. Think about offering choices.

hints.question: What if someone doesn't want to do any of the options I suggest?
hints.answer: That's okay! The best way to know is to ask them directly. They might have a creative idea you haven't thought of, or they might prefer a supporting role like cheering or observing.

hints.question: How can I make sure all roles feel equally important?
hints.answer: Clearly explain how each role contributes to the overall success or outcome of the activity. Emphasize that every contribution, big or small, is valuable to the team or project.

educatorNotes.sampleAnswer:
Activity: The Great Clue Hunt (Modified).
Instructions: Teams race to find hidden clues around the park and solve a puzzle. Here are different ways to participate:
1.  **Clue Runners**: Some team members can run to each clue location to retrieve it. (Benefits those who enjoy physical activity and speed).
2.  **Clue Readers/Solvers**: Others can stay at a central point, read the clues brought back, and work on solving the puzzle. (Benefits those who prefer less physical activity, enjoy reading, or problem-solving).
3.  **Answer Recorders**: Someone can be responsible for writing down the answers as they are solved. (Benefits those who enjoy writing and organizing information).
4.  **Map Navigators/Guides**: A team member can guide the runners to the clue locations using a map. (Benefits those who enjoy strategy and directing).
Every role is crucial for the team to find all clues and solve the puzzle!
educatorNotes.commonMisconception: A common misconception is that 'inclusive' means making an activity easier for everyone, rather than providing diverse ways to participate that leverage different strengths and preferences. Learners might simplify the main task instead of offering alternatives.
reviewChecks: At least 3 roles make a meaningful contribution.
Participants are asked what suits them and can request adjustments.
Roles are offered without assumptions about ability or preference.
educatorNotes.safetyNotes: When conducting activities involving art supplies, ensure proper ventilation for paints and glues. Supervise the use of sharp tools like scissors. Remind children to wash hands after handling materials.
